newsitem.title: MACEDONIA: MACEDONIAN LOCAL POLLS TEST RULING PARTY.
newsitem.headline: MACEDONIAN LOCAL POLLS TEST RULING PARTY.

text.p: Voters in Macedonia are due to pass judgment on the ruling party's pursuit of rapid free-market reforms when they go to the polls this weekend to elect municipal governments.
Analysts say Sunday's municipal elections are being treated like a national political contest between the ruling Social Democrats and the main opposition parties, led by the nationalist VMRO-DPMNE.

Voters face a choice between the opposition's promise of a slower pace of economic reform and closer ties with its old Eastern-bloc allies, and the Social Democrats drive to build a free-market, Western-leaning economy.
The two sides also differ over Greece, where a long-running dispute over Macedonia's name has damaged relations between Athens and Skopje.
The Social Democrats have taken a pragmatic approach and argued for compromise, while the opposition says Macedonia must protect its national identity through its name.

"The public might be going to vote for local councils and mayors, but the political parties are running a campaign that looks more like a national parliamentary election," said independent journalist Branko Geroski.
"They are not talking about rubbish collection or street lighting or other local issues, but about Macedonia's economic performance, its international position and so on," he said.
The Social Democrats are taking credit for Macedonia's transformation from a minor republic inside the former Yugoslav federation into an independent state with regional influence.
The country broke with Belgrade in September 1991 along with Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia, and faced its first parliamentary elections three years later.
The opposition parties, who boycotted the 1994 parliamentary elections, say if they win a majority of city councils they will demand that parliamentary polls, due by 1998, be held sooner.
To complicate the political landscape further, ethnic Albanians who dominate western districts are likely to vote for parties representing their own ethnic interests.
Diplomats fear ethnic tensions could worsen if nationalist Albanian parties do well in the election.
In a measure of the stakes involved, Prime Minister Branko Crvenkovski has taken personal charge of the Social Democrats' campaign, said one Western official who declined to be named.
"That means Crvenkovski will have to take responsibility for the results," said the Western analyst.
"If they get a good result, his position will be much stronger, but if they don't then we can expect some major changes to the party leadership and even the government."
The Social Democrats have laid on an expensive advertising campaign and big events designed to snatch media space.
Observers say the opposition parties were caught off-guard with an inadequate campaign machine and insufficient funds to counter the Social Democrats' blitz.
There have been few opinion polls over the past few months and even fewer surveys that independent analysts say give a clear idea of the likely outcome.

"I think the Social Democrats will get the most mayors," said Geroski. "But I think they won't get a majority and will probably even get a much smaller proportion of the vote that they got in the last parliamentary election."
